facts.text: Most of the film's Seattle locations were used illegally. The crew shot guerrilla-style at night, dodging the authorities.
The costume designer was jailed for unpaid parking tickets mid-shoot, and her car, packed with costumes for 20+ people, was impounded. Petty cash bailed her out.
It began as a short, Orpheus and Eurydice. Robert McGinley wanted other people to play Orpheus, then got talked into playing him himself.
Smoke machines once filled a building with so much haze that the Seattle Fire Department showed up with five trucks. The Coast Guard also confronted the crew.
Some skating shots were filmed with a 16mm camera mounted on a skateboard, rigged by action stunt photographer Stan Larson.
The band The Shredders was played by real Seattle musicians: Dennis Rea on guitar, Amy Denio on bass, Bill Rieflin on drums and Roland Barker on keys.
Composer Roland Barker and drummer Bill Rieflin were bandmates in the Seattle band the Blackouts. Both later joined industrial metal pioneers Ministry.
Amy Denio made her film debut here. Her bass playing shares the soundtrack with her bandmates, who all cut the score together.
Gian-Carlo Scandiuzzi, who plays Hades, later became executive director of Seattle's ACT Theatre.
Steven Jesse Bernstein, a legendary Seattle underground poet who recorded for Sub Pop, plays Axel. He died in 1991, a couple of years after the shoot.
Axel gets around on a longboard instead of a wheelchair. He doubles as a Greek-chorus narrator.
John Billingsley, who plays manager Linus, later became Dr. Phlox on Star Trek: Enterprise.
McGinley cited Videodrome, Mad Max 2 and Bones Brigade skate videos as influences on the film's look.
The Seattle International Film Festival rejected it in 1989. Then a Halloween midnight show at the Neptune Theater drew big crowds, and Landmark gave it a six-month Friday midnight run.
The film was shot on mixed formats, 16mm and video, then blown up to 35mm for theaters.
A blog commenter put the budget at about $160K. A cast of Seattle performance artists and skaters filled out the movie.
In 2014 Light in the Attic's Traction imprint pressed the soundtrack on vinyl, 17 songs, bundled with a DVD of the movie.
Vinegar Syndrome and AGFA's 2023 Blu-ray includes a commentary with McGinley and AGFA's Bret Berg, plus the original VHS version.
A novelization came out from Encyclopocalypse Publications in April 2025, with scenes from an earlier draft of the script.
One critic called it a love letter to independent artistry made when Seattle was still a backwater, before grunge and the dotcom boom.
